title: Step 10: External service: standards lookup with timeouts, retries, caching; outbound webhooks
summary: TraceLite calls a standards catalogue with a deadline per attempt, retries only what may go away, honors Retry-After within its own budget and serves a stale title rather than an error. It calls subscribers' webhooks the same way, signed with HMAC and carrying an event id that makes redelivery harmless.

examples.title: One attempt at the catalogue: its own timeout inside the caller's deadline, and what each answer means

annotations.note: Two errors callers test with errors.Is. ErrUnknownClause is an answer, which example 3 caches. errTransient marks what may go away; wrapping it with %w next to the cause keeps both visible.
context.WithTimeout derives from the caller's context, so an attempt ends at whichever comes first: its own 300 ms or the API request's deadline. TraceLite uses 2 s per attempt.
No answer at all (a refused connection, a reset, this attempt's timeout) is transient: the next attempt may well get through.
The status decides. 200 is the title, 404 an answer, 429 and 5xx may go away, and anything else is TraceLite's mistake, which no retry fixes.

A size limit on what is read back, so a broken catalogue can't make TraceLite read without end. The real catalogue answers JSON, and TraceLite decodes it without RejectUnknownMembers, unlike its own API: a client of someone else's API accepts members it doesn't know yet.
Retry-After is either a number of seconds or an HTTP date. This reads the seconds form; a date, or no header, counts as no wish at all.
The slow answer: the handler waits until the client gives up. The attempt fails after 300 ms whatever the catalogue does, which keeps the run deterministic.
The client's Timeout is only a backstop for code that forgets a context; http.DefaultClient has none. The client is built once and shared, so connections are reused.
The API request's budget: 2 s in all, shared by every attempt. The slow attempt spends 300 ms of it.

examples.title: Retrying what may go away: full jitter, Retry-After, and never a wait past the caller's deadline

annotations.note: The retry loop, as in go.services.retries: a bounded number of attempts, and a wait between them that the caller can cancel.
Only errTransient is retried. A 404 or a 400 fails the same way every time, so it returns at once.

Full jitter: a random wait between zero and a ceiling that doubles (200 ms, then 400 ms), so that many clients failing together don't retry together. Retry-After wins when it is longer; a server under load knows better.
A wait longer than the time left can only end in a timeout, so the loop gives up at once and the caller can fall back to its cache (example 3).

Three lookups: 503, a timeout, then 200 (three attempts, one answer); a 429 asking for 120 s against a 2 s budget; three 502s, which fail after the last attempt. The API answers 503 for the last two, unless the cache has an older title.

examples.title: The cache: answers for 24 hours, 404s for 10 minutes, and a stale title when the catalogue is down

annotations.note: One entry per reference. err holds ErrUnknownClause for a remembered 404, so a typo doesn't cost a call per keystroke.
Cache first. A fresh entry, including a remembered 404, answers without any call.
The call runs outside the lock: it may take the request's whole budget, and other lookups shouldn't wait for it. Two concurrent misses for one reference both call the catalogue (see Weaknesses).
An answer is kept for 24 hours, a 404 for 10 minutes, so a newly added clause appears soon.
The catalogue failed and an older title exists: it comes back marked stale. Degraded, not broken, and the UI can say so.
25 hours later the entry has expired, the catalogue fails, and the lookup returns the old title with stale: true.

examples.title: Outbound webhooks: one body signed per attempt; the receiver checks the MAC, the time and the event id

annotations.note: The envelope. id is minted once per event, when the failed run is recorded, and stays the same across every retry to every subscriber: it is the key receivers deduplicate by. data is abridged here.
go.services.webhooks-hmac's scheme: the timestamp is part of the signed bytes, so a captured request can't be replayed with a new time. Each webhook has its own secret.

sync.Map's LoadOrStore checks and records an id in one step, safe for concurrent requests. A real receiver inserts the id into a table in the transaction that does the work, with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING.
The header is "t=<unix seconds>,v1=<hex>". A malformed one leaves got empty, which can't match any MAC.
The receiver checks the HMAC over the raw bytes with hmac.Equal, which doesn't leak timing information, and refuses timestamps more than five minutes away from its own clock.

Deduplication by event id is the receiver's half of idempotency: TraceLite will deliver some events twice, and this is where twice becomes once. The duplicate still gets a 2xx, or the sender would keep trying.
Marshaled once: every attempt sends the same bytes. Marshaling again could even change them: encoding/json/v2 writes map entries in no particular order unless the Deterministic option is set.
Signed at each attempt, so the timestamp is fresh and a retry minutes later still falls inside the receiver's window.
The lost response: attempt 1 was processed, but its answer never reached TraceLite, which timed out and sent attempt 2. The receiver recognizes the id and does nothing twice.

Someone without the secret, and a captured request replayed later: both 401. The id check would catch the replay too, but only while the receiver still remembers the id; the window means it has to remember ids for minutes, not forever.

use_cases: Enriching your data from a third-party catalogue: standards, postal codes, exchange rates, VAT numbers
Notifying CI, chat or ticketing systems when a test run fails
Any server-to-server call where the other side can be slow, rate-limited or down for an hour
Keeping a page usable while a dependency is down, by showing slightly old data marked as such
strengths: Every call is bounded by the caller's deadline, so a slow catalogue slows the detail page by at most its budget and never hangs a handler
Full jitter spreads retries from many clients, and Retry-After is honored, so a struggling service isn't hammered back down
Cached answers, including 404s, cut traffic to the catalogue to roughly one call per reference per day
HMAC signatures with a timestamp and per-event ids give receivers authenticity, replay protection and exactly-once processing on top of at-least-once delivery
weaknesses: The in-memory cache is per process and empties on restart; several TraceLite instances would each call the catalogue
Concurrent misses for the same reference each call the service; golang.org/x/sync/singleflight would merge them into one call
In-process webhook retries die with the process; durable delivery needs the job table of step 11
Webhook URLs come from users, so the server makes requests to addresses users chose; a multi-user deployment must refuse private and loopback targets

pitfalls.title: http.DefaultClient and no context
pitfalls.detail: DefaultClient has no timeout, and a request without a deadline can hang a handler until the TCP connection dies. Derive a per-attempt context from the caller's.
pitfalls.good: ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(r.Context(), 2*time.Second); defer cancel(); req, _ := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, "GET", u, nil)

pitfalls.title: Retrying everything
pitfalls.detail: A 400 or 403 fails the same way every time, and a retried POST without an idempotency key may run twice. Retry timeouts, 429 and 5xx, and only operations that are safe to repeat.

pitfalls.title: Sleeping past the deadline
pitfalls.detail: A Retry-After of 120 s inside a 2 s request budget only produces a timeout two seconds later. Compare the wait with ctx.Deadline() and give up, or serve from the cache, at once.

pitfalls.title: Re-encoding the event per attempt
pitfalls.detail: Building the body again for a retry can change it: a new timestamp, or map entries in another order (encoding/json/v2 doesn't sort them unless the Deterministic option is set). Marshal once, sign per attempt, send the same bytes.

pitfalls.title: Treating a timeout as a failure to deliver
pitfalls.detail: A webhook that timed out may have been processed. Retry it with the same event id, and expect receivers to deduplicate; never mint a new id for a retry.

quiz.q: The catalogue answers 429 with Retry-After: 120, and the API request has 2 s left. What does the client do?
options: Gives up at once, and serves the cached title if there is one
quiz.why: Waiting longer than the budget can only end in a timeout. The client compares the wait with its deadline, and Lookup falls back to a stale entry.

quiz.q: A webhook delivery times out. Was the event processed?
options: Maybe: the receiver may have processed it and the answer been lost
quiz.why: That is why delivery is at least once, retries reuse the event id, and receivers deduplicate on it.

quiz.q: Why is a 404 from the catalogue cached?
options: So that repeated lookups of a wrong reference don't each call the service; for 10 minutes, not 24 hours
To return it as stale later
quiz.why: A negative answer is still an answer. A shorter lifetime lets a newly added clause appear soon.

quiz.q: Why is the timestamp inside the HMAC rather than only in a header?
options: So a captured request can't be replayed later with a fresh timestamp
quiz.why: If the time weren't signed, an attacker could change it freely and pass the receiver's tolerance check forever.

body:
## Concept

TraceLite talks to two kinds of outside services, and is polite to both the same way:

- **A standards catalogue it calls.** Requirements cite clauses of standards
  (`ISO27001:A.5.17`). Step 6's detail view gains a lookup that shows a clause's title,
  fetched through `GET /api/standards/{ref}`, which calls the catalogue. The browser never
  calls it directly: that would need CORS, would expose any API key, and would bypass the
  cache.
- **Webhooks it calls on behalf of users.** A project can register URLs that receive a
  signed POST when a test run fails, so a CI system or a chat channel hears about it.

Politeness has the same four parts in both directions:

1. **Bound every call.** A deadline per attempt, derived from the caller's context, and a
   size limit on what is read back.
2. **Retry only what may go away**, and only operations that are safe to repeat: network
   errors, timeouts, 429 and 5xx. Wait with jittered backoff, or as long as Retry-After
   asks, but never past the caller's deadline.
3. **Remember answers.** A cache with expiry turns a daily-changing catalogue into a
   daily call, and a stale entry beats an error when the service is down.
4. **Make repeats harmless.** A retried webhook carries the same event id; receivers
   deduplicate on it. HMAC signatures prove the request came from TraceLite.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java**: Resilience4j's Retry, TimeLimiter and a Caffeine cache are these pieces as
  annotations and decorators. Here each is a few visible lines, and the deadline comes
  from the incoming request's `context.Context` instead of a thread-local.
- **Python**: `requests` without `timeout=` waits forever, like `http.DefaultClient`;
  `urllib3.Retry(backoff_factor=..., respect_retry_after_header=True)` is the loop of
  example 2.
- **JS**: `fetch` with `AbortSignal.timeout(2000)` is `context.WithTimeout`;
  `AbortSignal.any([request, timeout])` composes the two deadlines that Go derives by
  passing the context down.
- **C/C++ (libcurl)**: `CURLOPT_TIMEOUT_MS` per transfer plus your own retry loop; the
  shape is the same, the context that ties it to the caller's budget is not.

## How it works

The catalogue behind TraceLite's own endpoint:

```yaml
  /api/standards/{ref}:
    parameters: [{ name: ref, in: path, required: true, schema: { type: string, maxLength: 64 } }]
    get:
      operationId: getStandardClause
      responses:
        "200":
          description: The clause; stale is true when the catalogue was unreachable and the title comes from the cache
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: object
                required: [ref, title, stale]
                properties: { ref: { type: string }, title: { type: string }, stale: { type: boolean } }
        "404": { $ref: "#/components/responses/Problem" }   # the catalogue has no such clause
        "503": { $ref: "#/components/responses/Problem" }   # unreachable and nothing cached
```

The catalogue's URL and key come from configuration (`TRACELITE_STANDARDS_URL`), not from
the repo; the client is built once in `cmd/tracelite` and shared by every request.

Webhooks are registered per project, in `migrations/003_webhooks.sql`:

```sql
-- +goose Up
CREATE TABLE webhooks (
  id         uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuidv7(),
  project_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES projects ON DELETE CASCADE,
  url        text NOT NULL CONSTRAINT webhooks_url_valid CHECK (url ~ '^https?://'),
  secret     text NOT NULL, -- the HMAC key; the receiver holds the same one
  events     text[] NOT NULL DEFAULT '{test-run.failed}'
               CONSTRAINT webhooks_events_valid CHECK (events <@ '{test-run.failed}'),
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX webhooks_project ON webhooks (project_id);
```

- The secret is stored in clear because TraceLite must compute HMACs with it; a hash
  would be useless. `events` lists the types a subscriber wants, constrained to the ones
  that exist, so a later type is added by replacing the CHECK. Deleting a project
  cascades to its webhooks.
- One event type so far, `test-run.failed`, published by the service after a failed run
  has been committed. Body: `{"id", "type", "createdAt", "data": {"projectId", "testCase",
  "requirements", "finishedAt"}}`, marshaled once (example 4).
- The dispatcher sends it to every webhook of the project that lists the type
  (`WHERE project_id = $1 AND $2 = ANY (events)`). Each POST is an attempt like example
  1's: its own timeout (10 s) derived from the caller's context, the shared client, and
  the response body read (bounded) and closed, because the Transport reuses a keep-alive
  connection only after the body was read to the end and closed.
- Header `TraceLite-Signature: t=<unix seconds>,v1=<hex HMAC-SHA256 of "<t>.<body>">`,
  computed for each attempt, and `Content-Type: application/json`. Receivers check the
  MAC and a five-minute window, and deduplicate on `id` (example 4).
- Responses: 2xx delivered. 410 Gone is the receiver saying "stop, for good", so the
  webhook is deleted (`DELETE FROM webhooks WHERE id = $1`). 429, 5xx and timeouts are
  retried with a loop like example 2's: delivery is at least once, since a timeout means
  "maybe processed". Any other 4xx stops this delivery: the receiver refused the request,
  and sending it again won't change its mind.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant S as TraceLite service
  participant D as Dispatcher
  participant R as Receiver
  S->>D: Publish(project, test-run.failed, id e1)
  D->>R: POST, TraceLite-Signature t=...,v1=...
  R->>R: verify, process e1, remember e1
  R--xD: (the response is lost)
  D->>D: attempt 1 timed out: wait, retry
  D->>R: POST, same body, fresh signature
  R-->>D: 200, e1 seen before, nothing done
```

## Design notes

**Stale beats broken.** The clause title is decoration on the detail page; showing
yesterday's title with a "stale" flag is better than an error box. Data that must be
current (a payment status, a permission) would fail closed instead. The choice is per
call, and the `Stale` field makes it visible to the UI rather than hiding it.

**A circuit breaker, not yet.** When a dependency is down for minutes, every request
still spends its first attempt finding out. A circuit breaker would skip the call for a
while after repeated failures. With a cache that serves most lookups and a 2 s budget,
TraceLite doesn't need one; the retry and cache code is where one would go.

**Webhooks belong in the job table.** Step 10's dispatcher retries in memory for a few
seconds. Real receivers are down for hours, and TraceLite restarts. Step 11 turns each
delivery into a row in a job table, inserted in the same transaction as the failed run
(so a committed run always gets its webhook, an outbox), with `run_after` holding the
next retry time on a schedule of minutes to hours. The signing, the event id and the
status handling stay exactly as here.

**User-chosen URLs.** A webhook URL makes TraceLite's server send requests wherever a user
points it. On a single-user local install that is the user's own business; a shared
deployment must resolve the host and refuse loopback, private and link-local addresses
before connecting, or a webhook becomes a way to reach internal services.
